title: From Thanks to Giving: Introducing the US Historic Preservation Training Fund
content:
This Thanksgiving, we’re grateful for the people who keep America’s history alive.This history  lives in more than its nationally recognized monuments. It lives in neighborhood museums, historic houses, community archives, cultural landscapes, oral histories, family collections and living traditions, from crafts to celebrations. Behind each of these are people working to ensure that their community’s places and stories, landscapes, recipes and traditions are preserved.

Many of these cultural heritage stewards work in small organizations like historical associations and local museums with limited funding, few staff, and growing responsibilities. They must care for collections and buildings, raise funds, engage their communities, respond to risks and ensure that the place, practices, and stories they protect remain accessible to future generations. Recent bi-partisan legislation has created more uncertainty about funding and new challenges for historic preservation.

title: HERITΛGE joins MusicSphere partners in Valencia
content:
On 2–3 November 2026, HERITΛGE met with the MusicSphere consortium in Valencia, Spain, for the project’s Fourth General Meeting which took place alongside the 23rd EuroXR International Conference (3–6 November 2026), bringing partners together at one of Europe’s leading events for extended reality research and practice.

MusicSphere – A Multimodal Approach for Digitizing, Analyzing, and Simulating Traditional Musical Organs Through 3D Technologies, Acoustic Analysis and Interactive Experiences – is a 42-month research and innovation project funded by the European Union’s Horizon Europe programme. It is part of the European Collaborative Cloud for Cultural Heritage (ECCCH), the EU initiative managed by the ECHOES project, and is coordinated by the Centre for Research & Technology Hellas (CERTH) in Thessaloniki, Greece.

title: HERITΛGE delivers Seasonal School on heritage adaptation to climate change
content:
Working with Prof. Brimblecombe

How can climate projections help heritage professionals decide which monument needs attention first? And what does adaptation mean for a mountain community whose landscape and traditions are threatened by recurring wildfires? These were among the questions that heritage professionals and researchers brought to Athens for the first Seasonal School of the European Partnership for Resilient Cultural Heritage (RCH).

The Heritage Management Organization (HERITΛGE) delivered the school, Heritage Adaptation to Climate Change, from 5 to 15 October 2026. More than 400 applications were filed from around the world. Fourteen participants attended in person at the European Parliament’s Europa Experience in Athens, and more than 100 took part online. The in-person participants were selected from candidates nominated by states participating in RCH. They represented 13 countries, with two participants from Spain and one each from Belgium, Croatia, Egypt, Finland, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania and the United Kingdom.

title: Australian heritage: A letter from Bologna
content:
Aboriginal painting on rock surfaces. Photo: Herbert Basedow, Public domain. Source: National Museum of Australia via Wikimedia Commons

By Olivia Panetta*

In May 2020, Rio Tinto legally destroyed two rock shelters at Juukan Gorge in the Pilbara region.  The shelters preserved evidence of approximately 46,000 years of occupation and held profound  cultural significance for the Puutu Kunti Kurrama and Pinikura peoples. Australian legislation made this destruction entirely legal. It occurred specifically under ministerial consent granted through Western Australia’s Aboriginal Heritage Act 1972. That is perhaps the most disturbing part: a place of extraordinary cultural importance and memory could be recognised and recorded and still  the law enabled a mining company more authority over the site than it gave the people to whom the place belonged. A parliamentary inquiry followed, recommending a national framework built on free, prior and informed consent. More than six years later, such reform has not yet been enacted.

title: Introducing our Online Academy: Build your skills and learn at your own pace.
content:
The Heritage Management Organization is expanding its training offer. With the launch of the HERITΛGE Online Academy, our specialist training is now available to everyone, to study in their own time.

Learning that fits around your life

Developing your skills should be possible alongside the demands of work and everyday life. With the Academy, you choose a course, enrol directly with no interview, and work through the materials when it suits you. There are no scheduled classes. You decide when to study within your course’s access period.

If you already know our trainer-led online workshops, the Academy offers a new way to learn with us. It complements our existing programmes with courses you can take on your own, without waiting for a workshop date or fitting your schedule around live sessions.

Practical knowledge for your heritage work

We’re launching with six subject areas. Each was designed with heritage organisations and their needs in mind, and curated jointly by our international faculty and our education team:

  • Heritage interpretation: communicate heritage through engaging narratives, talks and walks.

title: Oral History and Heritage workshop in Monterrey
content:
On October 8 and 9, HERITΛGE held the in-person Oral History and Heritage workshop at the Museo Estatal de Culturas Populares de Nuevo León. The workshop – part of our HerMaP Mexico initiative – provided a space for learning and exchange focused on the use of oral history to document, preserve, and transmit cultural heritage and community memory. The program combined methodological tools, ethical considerations, and practical exercises applied to heritage projects.

The workshop brought together a group of eight participants working with Indigenous communities and cultural heritage projects, bringing diverse experiences and perspectives and representing at least five Indigenous peoples residing in Nuevo León. This exchange provided an opportunity to reflect on oral history not only as a documentation methodology, but also as a tool for strengthening the transmission of memories, knowledge, and living cultural practices.

title: Trainees explore Community Engagement
content:
How can heritage practitioners create meaningful opportunities for communities to shape the ways their heritage is understood, cared for and shared? This question guided HERITΛGE’s recent four-day online workshop, Engaging Communities in Cultural Heritage, which brought together 23 participants from 18 countries.

Participants joined from Poland, Lebanon, Italy, Iraq, Albania, Greece, Armenia, Rwanda, Serbia, Latvia, Mauritius, India, Egypt, Iran, South Africa, Kenya, Palestine and Nepal to explore 

The programme examined different understandings of community, identity, belonging and relationships with heritage, while emphasising the importance of positionality, research, inclusion, accessibility and meaningful participation. 

Participants were introduced to approaches including Asset-Based Community Development, asset mapping and ethnographic research, exploring how community assets, knowledge, relationships and networks can inform the design and implementation of engagement activities.

title: Celebrating European Heritage Days at the RCH launch in Marseille
content:
Alexandre Causse from RCH Co-ordinator FSP declaring the opening of the Kick off event

The Heritage Management Organization (HERITΛGE) marked this year’s European Heritage Days by joining our fellow consortium partners and hundreds of cultural heritage and climate professionals, researchers, policymakers and other stakeholders from around the world for the launch of the European Partnership for Resilient Cultural Heritage (RCH) in Marseille, France. RCH is co-funded by the European Union. 

With the 2026 European Heritage Days theme, “Heritage at Risk: Revive, Resist, Reimagine,” the gathering offered a timely opportunity to turn attention towards the future of heritage in a changing climate—and the role heritage itself can play in helping communities adapt.

title: A visit to Red Rock Centre in Rwanda
content:
Mark chatting to community members in the Red Rocks centre.

By Mark Goldstone* 

Ochre burnt-orange dust, which for convenience we call red, covers both the outside and the inside of my 4×4. Everything is a hill in Rwanda, and my trip today takes me up a thousand hills and down a thousand more. Power takes me up and gravity takes me down like a marble in a marble run. 

My destination is the Red Rocks Intercultural Exchange Centre in Rwanda’s highlands outside the city of Musanze. The journey is hard and I arrive tired and dusty, but within five minutes every member of staff knows my name. This is the kind of welcome you can expect at Red Rocks, a community-based initiative  working with communities living alongside protected areas and important natural ecosystems that has received one of HERITΛGE’s small grants for African projects and is also the recipient of another grant, fiscally sponsored by HERITΛGE.

title: 10 proyectos de patrimonio del norte de México reciben apoyos
content:
The Heritage Management Organization (HERITΛGE) se complace en anunciar los 10 proyectos seleccionados para recibir apoyo a través de HerMaP México, su principal iniciativa para fortalecer la gestión del patrimonio cultural en la región fronteriza del norte de México.

Los proyectos seleccionados representan a Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León y Tamaulipas, garantizando así la representación de los seis estados que conforman el ámbito geográfico de HerMaP México en esta primera convocatoria de apoyos.

Los proyectos fueron seleccionados entre 115 solicitudes recibidas a través de una convocatoria abierta lanzada a principios de 2026, reflejando tanto la extraordinaria riqueza del patrimonio cultural de la región como el compromiso de las comunidades, profesionales e instituciones que trabajan para salvaguardarlo.
